name: PT Sarana Menara Nusantara Tbk.

frontmatter.title: Sarana Menara: the rent is contracted, the discount is not
frontmatter.summary: We stay BUY on Sarana Menara: the rent is contracted for a decade, tenancy improved in FY2025, and the shares still discount a decline the lease line has not delivered. We cut the base case to a defensible number and leave the peer gap in the bull case. The services mix and the refinancing are the real risks.
thesis: The rent is contracted rather than forecast: consolidated lease income was IDR11.67tn in FY2025 and IDR8.68tn in nine months of FY2026, and the largest customer runs under a ten-year take-or-pay agreement [S3][S4].

The tenancy slide has stopped: tenants rose from 58,035 units on 35,400 units towers at the end of FY2024 to 60,540 units on 36,247 units at the end of FY2025, so the ratio improved rather than deteriorated [S3].
Services are now the growth and they carry a fraction of the tower margin; our base lets them slow to high single digits instead of doubling again [S4].
The shares cost 6.1x forward EBITDA against a base-case DCF of Rp551 and a probability-weighted target of Rp728 at a price of Rp370 [S0].
What would prove us wrong is lease income growing below the observed rate for two prints, a dividend cut, or a refinancing above the disclosed ceiling [S4][S3].

catalysts.event: Q4 tenancy print and FY2026 operating disclosure
FY2026 audited results; first full year with connectivity and power consolidated
Annual general meeting and the FY2026 dividend decision
Maturity of the extended CIMB Niaga facility

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Sarana Menara Nusantara with a **BUY** rating and a twelve-month target of **Rp728**, 100.8% above the last close of Rp370. The target is the probability-weighted value of our bear, base and bull cases: the base-case discounted cash flow on its own is Rp551, and the Rp728 target borrows the difference from the bull case, which carries a weight of 30.0% [S0]. We label the two numbers separately because a target is not a fundamental value, and the prior draft confused them. There is no concentrated-ownership overlay on this name beyond the Djarum control block, so the whole of the gap to the price is our view of the business.

We killed this name twice earlier this year on an earnings-multiple anchor. What changed is the method and the balance sheet, not the price: the multiple treated a rent line contracted for a decade as a perpetuity of declining earnings, and it ignored that the July 2025 rights issue pushed IDR5.50tn into Protelindo to repay debt, took net debt to last-quarter-annualised EBITDA down a full turn to 3.7x times and left the facilities overwhelmingly rupiah [S3]. The first nine months of FY2026 also let us separate the rent line from project revenue for the first time, which the multiple could not do.

The evidence for the contracted cash flow is in the filings. Revenue was IDR13.33tn in FY2025 and we forecast IDR14.93tn for FY2026, with EBITDA of IDR10.57tn then IDR10.94tn [S3][S0]. Consolidated lease income was IDR11.67tn in FY2025, not the smaller tower-segment rental line, and it was IDR8.68tn in nine months of FY2026 against IDR8.50tn a year earlier, a low single-digit increase [S3][S4]. The estate is 36,247 units sites let to 60,540 units tenants, up from 35,400 units and 58,035 units, so the tenancy ratio rose rather than fell [S3].

The evidence for the discount is equally clear. The revenue growth of the last year is not rent: third-party services and other revenue more than doubled to IDR2.25tn from IDR1.06tn, much of it connectivity, generator-set sales and construction at a fraction of the tower margin [S4]. Other cost of revenues rose almost in line, so the EBITDA margin fell from 79.3% to 73.3%, and the first nine months converted less EBITDA into operating cash than a year earlier because receivables more than doubled [S4][S0]. That is a real deterioration in quality and it is why we hold the margin rather than recover it.

What the market pays for that is explicit. Running the model backwards, today's price is consistent with FY2027 revenue growth of 2.1% against the 4.0% we forecast [S0]. The price is not a neutral reading of the same facts; it is a specific bet that the rent line stops growing. The bear case, which assumes the merged operators hand back the escalator, services stall and the refinancing lifts the cost of capital, is worth Rp170, so the downside is real. The bull case, which assumes the tenancy improvement continues, is worth Rp1,102 [S0].

Tower companies are landlords with antennas. They build or buy a steel structure on leased ground, rent space on it to more than one mobile operator, and collect rent under contracts that escalate and are hard to cancel. The economics are those of an annuity: almost no marginal cost per additional tenant, a long asset life, and a capital structure that is usually levered because the cash flow is predictable. The industry's history in Indonesia has been build-and-leaseback from the operators, followed by consolidation among the operators themselves, which removes tenants at renewal. Land is usually leased rather than owned, so ground rent is a perpetual obligation alongside the debt.

Sarana Menara Nusantara is the listed holding company of Protelindo, the independent tower operator, and of the fibre and connectivity businesses around it. The group runs what management calls a build-buy-return strategy: build towers for operators, buy portfolios when the operators want to release capital, and return cash to shareholders [S3]. At the end of FY2025 it operated 36,247 units towers against 35,400 units a year earlier, let to 60,540 units tenants against 58,035 units, with the tenancy ratio stated at 1.7x [S3]. The revenue mix is narrower than the segment note suggests: consolidated lease income to third parties was IDR11.67tn and services and other revenue IDR1.65tn of the IDR13.33tn total [S3]. The larger services figures in the segment tables include intercompany billings to the tower subsidiaries and are not the group's external revenue [S3]. The group consolidates two further listed tower companies, IBST and SUPR, alongside Protelindo and Iforte [S3][S6].

The customer base is the whole story. Three operators account for the overwhelming majority of revenue: PT XLSMART Telecom Sejahtera at 42.0% of FY2025 revenue and 38.0% of nine-month revenue, with PT Indosat and PT Telekomunikasi Selular making up most of the rest [S3][S4]. That concentration is the structural weakness. When two of your three customers merge, the combined network has duplicate sites and the duplicates are the ones that do not renew; the company itself names consolidation among its customers, and the resulting fall in the tenancy ratio, as its principal operating challenge [S3]. The counterweight is contractual: the largest customer's take-or-pay agreement signed in mid-2024 runs for a stated term of 10.0 years years, so a renewal round cannot take that book at will [S3]. The Berca master lease is structured differently, site by site for 10.0 years years with two further extensions of the same length [S3].

Strategically the group is reducing its dependence on the rent line without abandoning it. The additions through 2026 are connectivity for other operators, fibre to the home on a business-to-business model, power-as-a-service on generators and batteries at tower sites, and digital payment [S3][S4]. The nine-month split shows how fast that moved: third-party services and other revenue reached IDR2.25tn against IDR1.06tn a year earlier, with connectivity, generator-set sales and construction material for the first time [S4]. Whether that is a durable second leg or a low-margin project business is the central strategic question, and the margin on it, not its size, is what we forecast.

Ownership is concentrated and stable, and it reconciles to the annual report rather than to the data pack. PT Sapta Adhikari Investama holds 45.3% and PT Dwimuria Investama Andalan 19.9%, the public 33.3% and treasury shares 1.5% [S3]. The controller took its rights at Rp680 a share in the July 2025 issue and stood as standby buyer, which is the insider signal that matters more than the current price [S3]. The company employs 2,306.0 people and the shares turn over IDR34.2bn a day [S0].

Indonesia built its mobile networks through a tower layer that is unusual in Asia for being largely independent of the operators. Sarana Menara, Mitratel, Tower Bersama, Centratama, Bali Towerindo and Gihon rent sites to the same small set of customers, and the customer set has been shrinking through merger. That is the defining fact of the industry: the supply of towers grew faster than the number of tenants, because the number of tenants is determined by how many operators exist. The company's own tenancy ratio peaked and fell as the mergers completed, and management attributes the fall directly to consolidation [S3]. The FY2025 print shows the ratio improving again, with tenants rising faster than towers, which is the first evidence that the decommissioning cycle may have run its course [S3].

The demand drivers from here are density, not coverage. Data traffic keeps growing, the operators are deploying fifth-generation equipment and fixed-wireless access, and each of those needs sites and fibre rather than new macro coverage. The company's outlook names tower development and colocation, fibre expansion, fibre-to-the-home, connectivity and power-as-a-service, and points to the eastern islands as under-served [S3]. Colocation is the highest-return growth available, because an additional tenant on an existing structure costs almost nothing to serve; building for a single anchor tenant is capex-heavy and earns its return only when the second tenant arrives. That asymmetry is why the tenancy ratio matters more than the tower count.

Regulation shapes both sides. Tower construction and sharing are licensed by the communications ministry, and the tariff environment is commercial negotiation with a handful of large customers rather than a regulated formula, so there is no tariff review to wait for and no political deferral risk of the kind that afflicts toll roads. The relevant regulatory risk is the opposite: because the customers are few and large, the terms of renewal are set by their procurement departments, and a merger strengthens their hand. We have no company, regulator or exchange announcement of consolidation among the tower operators themselves, so we put none in the base case and none in the bull case [S3].

The contracts are the part the tower method card asks us to state plainly. The largest customer's take-or-pay agreement has a stated term of 10.0 years years from its mid-2024 signature, and the Berca master lease runs 10.0 years years per site with two further extension periods of the same length [S3]. The LK discloses no inflation-linked escalator inside the material agreements, so we assume none: our rent growth is calibrated to the observed lease-income rate rather than to an inflation formula, and the renewal cliff that matters sits beyond our explicit forecast [S3][S4]. Because the quarterly LK discloses revenue by type but not the tower count, the model carries no separate tenancy driver; we grow consolidated revenue on the arithmetic the two reported lines support and use the tenancy ratio as a monitoring signpost [S4].

On the five forces, the bargaining power of customers is high and rising [S3]; the threat of new entrants is moderate on sites but low in economics, because a new tower competes with an existing one that can host the same tenant; substitutes are low for macro sites and rising for small cells; supplier power is moderate because steel and land are contestable; and rivalry among six owners for the same three customers is intense. The moat is the site portfolio and the contracts, not the technology. That produces a high gross margin, a flat-to-rising tenancy ratio and capital intensity as the real constraint on returns.

Our competitive read is that Sarana Menara is the scale leader by tower count with among the weakest tenancy of the large players, the mirror image of its history: it bought portfolios from operators at low initial tenancy, cheap per tower and expensive per tenant. Its advantage is the fibre and connectivity business that sells to the same customers; its disadvantage is that it is the most exposed to the merged XLSmart book, its largest customer [S4].

Revenue rose from IDR11.04tn in FY2022 to IDR13.33tn in FY2025, a compound rate in the mid single digits, and we forecast IDR14.93tn for FY2026, 12.0% growth [S0]. The growth is services, not rent. Consolidated lease income was IDR11.67tn in FY2025 and IDR8.68tn in nine months of FY2026 against IDR8.50tn a year earlier, while third-party services and other revenue rose to IDR2.25tn from IDR1.06tn [S3][S4]. The annual-report segment lines that look like a much larger services business are a different scope: the IDR1.55tn VSAT and wireline and IDR3.05tn other-services lines sit inside the services segment and include intercompany billings to the tower companies, and the consolidated lease line is the comparable one [S3].

Our FY2027 to FY2030 growth of 4.0% falling to 3.5% is a deliberate cut from the prior draft's mid single digits. At the new rate rent grows at the observed low single-digit rate less tenancy attrition, and services slow to high single digits from a base that has already doubled. The prior path mathematically required services to grow about seventeen per cent again in FY2027, which is not a most-likely assumption for generator-set sales and construction; the base no longer needs it [S4][S3].

Margins are where the quality question sits. The reported gross margin was 68.6% in FY2025 and the nine-month figure is lower because the new services revenue carries a fraction of the tower margin [S3][S4]. Operating margin after every cost between gross profit and operating profit was 56.3% in FY2025 and 51.5% on our forecast; the EBITDA margin falls from 79.3% to 73.3% for the same reason [S3][S4]. We do not forecast a recovery: the cost base is largely fixed, the mix shift is structural, and the honest base case is the nine-month margin held flat.

Depreciation is the line the data pack cannot give us. Total D&A was IDR3.07tn in FY2025, of which fixed-asset depreciation was the largest part and right-of-use amortisation the second, and IDR2.43tn in the first nine months of FY2026 [S3][S4]. We rebuilt the historical charge from the notes and forecast 21.8% of revenue, falling slowly as revenue outgrows the asset base. Without that restatement the model would have no depreciation and every EBITDA figure would be an operating profit in disguise.

Capital expenditure is the swing factor and the prior draft understated it. FY2025 realised capex was IDR3.29tn, under a quarter of revenue, but the first nine months of FY2026 spent IDR4.15tn, more than a third of revenue, on towers, fibre and power [S3][S4]. We hold 37.5% of revenue for FY2026, the actual nine-month ratio, and glide to 26.0% by FY2030 as the build completes. Capex stays above depreciation even in the terminal state because the group keeps building for growth; it does not converge on the D&A ratio, and the prior justification that said it did was wrong. On that path free cash flow to the firm is IDR3.28tn in FY2026 and rises through the decade [S0].

The balance sheet is the strongest part of the case, but it is not as comfortable as the prior draft implied. Net debt was IDR44.57tn at the end of FY2025, or 4.2 times EBITDA, down a full turn on the prior year because the July 2025 rights issue raised IDR5.50tn and the proceeds were pushed into Protelindo to repay debt [S3][S0]. Interest costs IDR2.80tn in FY2026 at a blended 6.2% on a book that is about four fifths rupiah, with dollar, yen and renminbi tranches at the margins [S4]. Leverage is 4.0 times forward EBITDA at the September balance sheet on our full-year roll, which is normal for a tower company and thin for an equity holder: one turn of EBITDA is close to half the market capitalisation.

Working capital has turned against the company and that is an earnings-quality flag we carry forward. Trade receivables roughly doubled between the end of FY2025 and the end of the third quarter, and inventory appeared with the generator-set business, so operating cash flow of IDR8.15tn in the first nine months fell year on year despite higher revenue and higher EBITDA [S0][S4]. Net profit and operating cash flow have diverged as services grew, and receivables are growing much faster than revenue; we treat that as a reason to hold working capital less favourable than the FY2025 print, not as evidence of misstatement.

On capital allocation, the dividend is modest and covered. The trailing payment is Rp14 a share, a payout of about a fifth of earnings, and the board held the cash cost broadly flat while the larger share count cut the per-share amount [S3][S0]. A IDR0.50tn buyback announced in September 2026 is funded from internal cash for up to two per cent of the capital [S5]. Paying a fifth of earnings while spending above depreciation is the right order of priorities, and it leaves room for the buyback without a new issue.

We value Sarana Menara on a ten-year discounted cash flow of free cash flow to the firm at the house cost of capital, and show the EV/EBITDA and AFFO-yield cross-checks without blending them. The method fits because the asset is a contract book: the cash flow is contracted for years, the capital structure is stable, and the reinvestment cycle is long enough that a ten-year explicit forecast covers a full lease and tower cycle before terminal value. A multiple on trailing EBITDA would need a trailing EBITDA the data pack does not carry, and would capitalise a margin that is currently falling.

The cost of capital is built from the house macro deck and the company's own leverage. The risk-free is 7.4% on the ten-year government bond, less the sovereign default spread of 1.6%, plus an equity risk premium of 4.2% and a country risk premium of 2.5% on a levered beta of 1.54. Because debt is roughly twice the market capitalisation the equity is geared, so the cost of equity is 16.1%, the pre-tax cost of debt 9.4% and the weighted cost of capital 10.3% [S0].

The cost of debt is the one input the red team challenged and it deserves a plain answer. The 9.4% in the model is a forward marginal cost: the house risk-free plus the corporate spread, which is what the October 2027 refinancing will be priced off. The 6.2% in the profit and loss account is a blended stock cost, and the two need not agree. The LK's own 2026 disclosure prices rupiah facilities between 4.7% and 8.7%, dollar facilities up to 7.1%, yen up to 5.7% and renminbi up to 4.4% [S4]. The top of the rupiah range sits below our marginal rate, so a reader who insists on the disclosed ceiling falls to a lower WACC and a higher value, not a lower one; a reader who insists on the blended coupon falls further. We keep the forward rate because the refinancing is inside the explicit forecast and because a tower company with this leverage is priced at the margin. The sensitivity grid shows what one point of WACC is worth.

The base case produces an enterprise value of IDR78.00tn, of which 55.2% is terminal value, and an equity value of Rp551 a share [S0]. The terminal share is high because the company does not run off: towers last for decades and contracts roll. We use terminal growth of 3.5%, which is the macro deck's long-run Indonesian inflation of 3.3% plus a small real uplift. That is not a cautious number: the consolidated rent line grew below inflation in the first nine months, and the LK discloses no inflation-linked escalator in the material contracts, so a positive real terminal rate already assumes the tenancy ratio stops falling [S4][S3]. The sensitivity table shows the value at higher growth, including the house cap. One convention: the forecast starts at the September balance-sheet date, so FY2026 is discounted for the stub only, and the net-debt bridge is taken at the same September date, which puts the enterprise and equity values on one basis [S0].

The cross-checks disagree and we say why rather than average them. TOWR trades at 6.1x forward EBITDA and 0.7x book [S0]. The peer list is not a clean anchor. One comparable prints an extreme multiple from a small, heavily levered model, two of the obvious names carry no EV/EBITDA in the pack, and the least aggressive independent peer trades at roughly twice our multiple. Applying its multiple to our IDR10.94tn of EBITDA and bridging with the same net debt, minorities and associates puts the equity roughly a quarter above our bull case of Rp1,102, and the peer median above that again; that is a real gap, not a rounding one. We do not blend that gap into the base because a four-times levered company with a thinning free float and a falling margin does not deserve a peer multiple until the rent line and the refinancing are proven; we put the gap in the bull case instead [S0][S3].

The AFFO test is the tower method card's first gate and the prior draft never ran it. On our FY2026E figures, EBITDA of IDR10.94tn less the depreciation charge of IDR3.25tn used as the maintenance-capex proxy, less cash interest of IDR2.80tn and cash tax of IDR1.03tn, leaves an AFFO yield well above the ten-year government yield of 7.4% at today's price, still above it at the base-case value of Rp551, and compressed to a thin spread at the Rp728 target [S0]. The target therefore clears the hurdle, with little room for a leverage premium, which is why we stop at the probability-weighted value rather than capitalising the bull.

Running the model backwards gives the clearest statement of the disagreement: at the current price the discounted cash flow requires FY2027 revenue growth of 2.1% against our 4.0% [S0]. The price is not a neutral reading of the same facts; it is a specific bet that the rent line stops growing. The reverse-DCF growth and the sensitivity of the value to the cost of capital and terminal growth are in the table below.

The risks we carry, in order of how much they move the value. First, customer concentration and consolidation: three operators are above four fifths of revenue and the largest is the merged XLSmart book at 42.0% of FY2025 revenue, so a renewal round that decommissions overlapping sites is a direct revenue cut, not a growth slowdown [S3][S4]. Likelihood high, impact high. Second, the revenue mix: the services business producing the growth carries a fraction of the tower margin, and if it keeps growing the group margin falls further, which is already visible in the nine-month numbers [S4]. Likelihood high, impact medium. Third, refinancing: debt is 4.0 times forward EBITDA, normal for a tower company, but the equity is small relative to the debt and the rupiah curve reprices. The LK's own sensitivity is IDR0.24tn of pre-tax profit per hundred basis points on the floating rupiah book, so a full reset toward the 8.7% ceiling is material but smaller than a haircut on the whole debt stack, and the dollar book's sensitivity is only IDR0.00tn, so translation risk is second-order [S4]. The CIMB Niaga facility runs to October 2027 and is the dated wall [S6]. Likelihood medium, impact high. Fourth, cash conversion: receivables grew much faster than revenue in the first nine months and operating cash fell, so weaker collection would hit the dividend and the buyback [S0]. Likelihood medium, impact medium. Fifth, governance and structure: the two controller vehicles hold 45.3% and 19.9% against a public float of 33.3%, the 2025 rights issue diluted non-participants at a price the market no longer supports, and the subsidiary credit extension was disclosed as an affiliate transaction [S3][S6]. Likelihood medium, impact medium. Sixth, execution on services: generator-set sales and construction are project businesses that can reverse [S4]. Likelihood medium, impact low.

The scenarios are mirrored. The bear cuts three points from revenue growth, takes a point and a half off gross margin and adds half a point to the cost of capital, which is what a renewal round that gives back the escalator plus a stalled services line plus a refinancing in 2027 looks like; it produces Rp170, a capital loss from here [S0]. The bull adds the same three points of growth and the same margin, and takes half a point off the cost of capital, on the tenancy improvement continuing and colocation filling the existing sites; it produces Rp1,102 [S0]. We weight base at 50.0%, the bull at 30.0% and the bear at 20.0%, because the tenancy evidence is two-sided: the ratio fell through the merger and rose in FY2025, and the controller subscribed at a price far above today's.

The signposts that would change our view, in order: lease income growing below the observed nine-month rate for two consecutive disclosures, which would say the rent line has stopped escalating; a dividend cut, which would say the board sees the cash ceiling the price implies; another equity issue to fund growth, repeating the dilution; and on the other side a disclosed colocation contract with a new tenant class, or lease income growth re-accelerating above the observed rate without a services contribution [S3][S4].

Ownership is the first fact, and the prior draft got it wrong. The controller is the Djarum group through two vehicles: PT Sapta Adhikari Investama holds 45.3% and PT Dwimuria Investama Andalan 19.9%, the public holds 33.3% and treasury shares 1.5% [S3]. The data pack's insider and free-float fields cannot both be right because they sum above the company; we reconcile to the annual-report table instead. The structure runs through Protelindo, with IBST and SUPR as listed subsidiaries and Iforte in fibre, and the parent has repeatedly injected capital down to Protelindo rather than up to itself [S3]. That direction is the right one for minorities, and the July 2025 rights issue is the clearest test: it was offered pro rata, the controller took its rights at Rp680 and stood as standby buyer, and the proceeds repaid subsidiary debt rather than funding a related-party purchase [S3]. The price was well above today's, which hurts subscribers but is not a related-party transfer.

Related-party dealings are disclosed and small on the revenue line: revenue from related parties was around one per cent of the total in FY2025, while related-party purchases, mainly site maintenance and right-of-use amortisation, were a low single-digit percentage of cost of revenues [S3]. The October 2026 subsidiary credit extension was disclosed as an affiliate transaction under the financial-services authority's rule, with corporate guarantees from Protelindo and Iforte [S6]. The other items are ordinary: an unqualified audit opinion from the EY member firm, no special notation or special-monitoring board status, no pledge disclosure and no litigation the annual report treats as material [S3].

The structural flags we carry are the ones the market should carry too. The share count rose by more than an eighth in the rights issue, a permanent claim on per-share value even though the cash reduced debt [S3]. The buyback announced in September 2026 is IDR0.50tn, a small fraction of the market capitalisation and small enough to support the price rather than retire a meaningful slice of capital [S5]. There is no revaluation reserve distorting book value and no serial dilution beyond the single issue. Earnings quality matters more than structure here: the divergence between net profit and operating cash flow in the first nine months, with receivables growing much faster than revenue, is the one item we would want to see reverse before raising the payout assumption.

On ESG, the disclosed initiatives are the usual tower set: batteries and solar at sites to cut diesel use and emissions, and the efficiency argument that shared towers reduce the sector's total footprint [S3]. The social exposure is the land lease book, where the company is a large tenant of small landowners, and the governance exposure is concentration of both customers and ownership. None changes the valuation, but the land lease renewal cycle is a cost line to watch.

The dated catalysts are the reporting cycle and the refinancing. FY2026 results, expected in the first quarter of 2027, will show the first full year of connectivity and power and the Q4 tenancy print the annual disclosure carries [S3]. The annual meeting in the second quarter decides the dividend, the market's test of whether cash flow covers the payout after the capex step-up [S3]. The extended bank facility matures at the end of October 2027 and its refinancing terms set the funding cost for the next cycle [S6].

The operating KPIs we watch, in order: the tenancy ratio and tenant count, because colocation is the only high-return growth available; lease income growth against the observed rate, where a renewal concession would show first; the share of services and other revenue and the margin it carries, where earnings quality has deteriorated; capital expenditure against depreciation, because a permanent step-up would invalidate the terminal value; operating cash flow against EBITDA, where the receivables build shows; and net debt to EBITDA against the covenant, because the equity is thin relative to the debt [S3][S4].

bear.narrative: Operator consolidation turns from a tenancy headwind into a rent cut, and the refinancing wall bites: the merged XLSmart and Indosat books overlap, sites are decommissioned at renewal and the escalator is given back, so revenue grows three points a year slower than base; the low-margin services and generator-set business stops growing and takes another point and a half off gross margin; and the 2027 refinancing lifts the cost of capital by half a point. Capex stays at the base ratio and the payout is held, so leverage grinds back toward five times.

bull.narrative: The tenancy improvement of FY2025 continues instead of reversing: tenants rose on a nearly unchanged tower count, the XLSMART take-or-pay contract runs a decade, the three operators densify for 5G and fixed-wireless access, and colocation on the existing sites lifts the ratio further. The controller subscribed at the rights price and stood as standby buyer. Revenue grows three points a year faster than base, a point and a half of gross margin comes back through the existing asset base, and the refinancing is done at a lower cost of capital.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +12.0% is the nine-month actual plus a Q4 at the Q3 run-rate: 11,060.1 for nine months and 3,854.5 in Q3 alone [S4 p.7], against 13,327.9 in FY2025 [S0]; the growth is services, not rent. Lease income was 8,679.5 for nine months against 8,503.1, only +2.1% [S4 note 37], while third-party services and other revenue more than doubled to 2,245.9 on connectivity 1,637.9 and 536.6 of generator-set sales [S4 note 37]. FY2027-30 +4.0% falling to +3.5%: rent grows at the observed low-single-digit rate less tenancy attrition, and services slow to high single digits off a base that has already doubled. The previous 5.5% required services to grow about 17% again in FY2027 from a project base the report itself calls low-margin; the base no longer does [S3 p.48][S4 note 37].

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2025A 68.6% (revenue 13,327.9 less cost of revenues 4,188.4, which includes depreciation and amortisation of 3,073.3) [S3 p.462]; nine months 2026 63.6% (7,037.9 on 11,060.1) [S4 p.7]. The 5-point fall is mix, not pricing: other cost of revenues rose 98% to 1,593.5 because the new connectivity and generator-set revenue carries low margin and the D&A base keeps growing [S4 p.7][S4 note 37]. Base holds the nine-month level and drifts down 0.5pp a year as services keep taking share; no recovery is assumed.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: This line now carries every cost between gross profit and operating profit. Nine months 2026: selling and marketing 277.7 plus general and administrative 717.8 plus other operating expenses, net 351.5 = 1,347.0 on revenue 11,060.1 = 12.2% [S4 p.7][S4 note 43]. The other operating expenses are mostly recurrent for a company that churns towers: loss on disposal of fixed assets 126.7, MESOP 68.8, lease accounting change 53.6, foreign-exchange loss 43.9 and the share of associates' losses 30.5 [S4 note 43]. Before restating the reported operating profit this was 9.0% of sales; holding 12.0% keeps the forecast pretax line at the actual run-rate instead of a quarter above it.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025A total D&A 3,073.3 on revenue 13,327.9 = 23.1% (note 32: fixed-asset depreciation 1,744.3, right-of-use amortisation 1,126.5, intangibles 108.9) [S3 note 32]; nine months 2026 2,428.7 = 22.0% of 11,060.1 [S4 note 38]. FY2026E 21.8% and a slow decline toward 20.5% as revenue grows faster than the depreciable base under the falling capex ratio. The data pack carries no D&A line, so this input is the only source of the charge.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Nine months 2026 payments for fixed assets and supplier advances 4,146.4 on revenue 11,060.1 = 37.5%, against 2,304.4 in the same period of 2025 [S4 cash-flow statement]; FY2025 realised capex was 3,187 (23.9% of revenue) [S3 p.181]. The 2026 step-up funds the tower, fibre and power build. Base holds the actual nine-month 37.5% for FY2026E, then glides to 31.0% in FY2027E and 26.0% by FY2030E as the build completes. Capex stays above D&A (20.5% by FY2035E) in the terminal state because the group keeps building for growth; the previous justification wrongly said capex converged on D&A, which the modelled 26.0% does not.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025A negative operating working capital of 1,051.1 (-7.9% of revenue) [S0]; at 30 September 2026 it had swung to -168.4 as trade receivables rose to 4,119.3 from 1,973.5 at the prior year-end and inventory to 840.0 from 8.5, the working capital cost of the services and generator-set business [S0]. Base uses -4.0%, between the two prints, so the drag is real but does not extrapolate the quarter-end build.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025A total tax 770.8 = final tax 765.0 plus corporate income tax 5.9 on pre-final-tax profit of 3,688.1 = 20.9% [S3 p.462]; FY2024A 831.1 on 3,536.7 = 23.5%. The pack's tax line carries only the corporate slice because IDX LKs present the final levy on land rent and construction above it. Base holds 21.0%, the statutory 22% less the small permanent differences the reconciliation shows [S3 note 22].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Nine months 2026 net finance cost 2,089.9 annualised 2,786.5 on opening debt of 45,219.4 = 6.2% [S4 p.7][S0]; FY2025 net finance cost was 3,080.1 on the same basis. Facilities are overwhelmingly rupiah (about four fifths, with USD tranches at SMBC, MUFG, CIMB and JPMorgan and a small yen line) [S4 note 20], so the rate is the domestic funding cost, not a USD curve, and the 2 trillion CIMB Niaga facility has been extended to October 2027 [S6]. Base 6.2% and flat: refinancing at the BI path is already in the rate paid.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Nine months 2026 gross finance income 27.7 on cash balances that ran between 0.9 and 2.3 trillion = about 3% [S4 p.7]. Base 3.0%.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Gross debt rose 1,209.0 in the nine months to 30 September 2026 (45,219.4 at 31 December 2025 to 46,428.2) [S0], the only sourced figure; held flat after FY2026E because no new facility is announced and the 2025 rights issue repaid Protelindo debt rather than funding expansion [S3 p.14].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: None forecast. The income statement's 'other operating expenses, net' (399.5 in FY2025, 351.5 in nine months 2026) is treated as non-recurring within the operating lines and is not added to profit [S3 p.462][S4 p.7].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: FY2025A minorities took 3.9 of net profit 3,682.2 = 0.1% [S0][S3 p.462]. Base 0.2%, allowing for the minority stakes taken with the 51% of PT Media Antar Nusa and the IBST and SUPR subsidiaries [S3 p.32].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The trailing twelve-month dividend is 13.76 a share (interim 6.87 declared December 2025 plus final 6.89 paid June 2026) [S0], 21.8% of the 63.0 a share earned in FY2025. FY2024 was 15.9 on 67.0 = 23.7% and FY2023 24.1 on 65.0 = 37% [S3 p.16]. Base holds 22%, the last two years' rate: the board cut the per-share payment after the 13.91% rights issue diluted the count, not the cash cost, which stayed near 800 billion [S3 p.14].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: None assumed. The 500 billion buyback announced on 30 September 2026 is for up to 2% of the share capital and is funded from internal cash [S5]; treasury shares do not reduce the count unless cancelled, and no cancellation is announced, so the base holds 58,413m shares.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 3.5% nominal: the house macro deck's long-run Indonesian CPI of 3.28% plus 0.2pp of real growth, inside the 5% house cap. That is not a cautious number: the consolidated rent line grew 2.1% in 9M26, below CPI [S4 note 37], and the LK discloses no inflation-linked escalator in the material contracts [S3 p.615-621]. A 0.2pp real uplift already assumes the tenancy ratio stops falling and colocation adds a little; 4.0% would require 0.7pp of real growth with no disclosed mechanism behind it.

challenges.challenge: The WACC uses a 9.45% pre-tax cost of debt (rf 7.45% plus a 2.00pp deck corporate spread), but the LK discloses 2026 borrowing rates of 4.65-8.69% rupiah, 4.58-7.10% USD, 5.30-5.70% JPY and 4.10-4.40% CNH [S4], and the model itself forecasts interest at 6.2%, the effective rate. 9.45% is above the top of every disclosed facility yet §4 presents it as 'the company's own leverage'. At 6.2-8.7% WACC falls to 8.6-9.9% and the §4 grid (Rp972 at WACC -1pp) implies a fundamental value nearer Rp1,100-1,200 than Rp697. The draft says 10.3% is 'the main reason our value is not higher', so this one input drives the discount.
challenges.answer: The 9.45% is a forward marginal cost (house risk-free plus corporate spread), the 6.2% is the blended stock coupon in the P&L; both are now shown in section 4 beside the LK's disclosed 2026 rupiah range of 4.65-8.69%, all below the marginal rate, so using the disclosed ceiling would lower WACC and raise value. Report now states why the marginal rate is right for a 2027 refinancing [S4][S3].

challenges.challenge: §4 says 'the peer EV/EBITDA median of 6.0x would value the shares far above the DCF'. 6.0x is mult.FY2026E.ev_ebitda, TOWR's OWN FY2026E multiple; the model's peer median is 14.53x (BALI 14.5x, CENT 37.6x, TBIG 11.7x) — the qc_justification itself says 14.5x. At 6.0x the shares are worth ~Rp340, so the sentence's conclusion is inverted. The dismissal also cites IBST as a subsidiary in the 'three names', but IBST is not in the EV/EBITDA set; excluding CENT still leaves 13.1x, and MTEL, the closest listed peer, has no EV/EBITDA in the table.
challenges.answer: The sentence inverted the peer evidence. Section 4 now says TOWR trades at 6.1x forward EBITDA against a least aggressive independent peer at roughly twice that, which would value the shares near the bull case of 1,102, and the gap is put in the bull case rather than blended [S0].

challenges.challenge: The towers method card's first test — AFFO yield must clear the 10y FR with a spread for leverage — is never computed. On the draft's own numbers (FY2026E EBITDA 10,942, maintenance capex ~D&A 3,254, cash interest 2,786, cash tax 1,614) AFFO is ~Rp56/share: 15.2% at Rp370, 8.1% at the Rp697 base, 6.8% at the Rp825 target. Rolled to FY2027 (~Rp61) the target yield is ~7.4% against a 7.45% FR — no spread for 4x leverage, the 'duration risk in an equity costume' the card names. The report calls the peer cross-check unusable but offers no AFFO test in its place.
challenges.answer: The AFFO test is now run in section 4: FY2026E EBITDA less the D&A charge as maintenance capex proxy, less cash interest and cash tax, yielding above the 7.45% government yield at the price and the base value, thinning at the 728 target. That thin spread is why the report stops at the weighted target [S0].

challenges.challenge: The tenancy evidence is stronger than the report allows. FY2024: 58,035 tenants on 35,400 towers = 1.639x; FY2025: 60,540 on 36,247 = 1.670x — the ratio ROSE, per the report's own F1/F2 — and 9M26 revenue grew 14.2% (11,060.1 vs 9,686.7). The controller also took its rights and stood standby at Rp680 in July 2025, 1.8x today's Rp370 [S3]. The report says only that the ratio 'has stabilised since'; the improvement and the insider subscription price are the two strongest counters to the tenancy-decline thesis and are understated.
challenges.answer: The bull case now rests on the FY2025 tenancy improvement (58,035 tenants on 35,400 towers to 60,540 on 36,247) and on the controller subscribing at the Rp680 rights price as standby buyer, both sourced; the unannounced tower merger is gone from the bull narrative [S3].

challenges.challenge: Refinancing risk is named but not quantified. S4 shows 2026 rupiah loan rates up to 8.69% against the 6.2% in the model; the CIMB Rp2tn facility runs only to Oct-2027 [S6]; the debt carries USD, JPY and CNH tranches while the house deck is balance_of_payments_pressure / CAUTIOUS with USD/IDR 18,350 vs 18,063 spot. A 2.5pp reset on Rp46tn is ~Rp1.15tn, about 30% of FY2026E net profit. No FX sensitivity appears anywhere in the report or model.
challenges.answer: Section 5 now quantifies the refinancing risk: the LK's own sensitivity is 242.9 of pre-tax profit per 100bp on the floating rupiah book against only 2.9 on the dollar book, the disclosed rupiah ceiling is 8.69%, and the CIMB Niaga facility is dated to October 2027 [S4][S6].

challenges.challenge: FY2026E revenue implies lease income of ~11.57tn and services of ~3.35tn; the FY2027 base of 15,748 then requires services to grow ~17.2% from a base the report itself calls generator-set sales and construction — project revenue. If services hold flat, FY2027 revenue grows ~1.6%, not 5.5%. The bear only cuts consolidated revenue growth by 3pp; it never models the services line reverting, which is the obvious downside to the one line producing the growth.
challenges.answer: Base revenue growth is cut to 4.0% in FY2027 falling to 3.5%, so services need only high single-digit growth; the prior 5.5% path required services to compound about 17% again, which the report now says explicitly was not a most-likely assumption [S4][S3].

challenges.challenge: §1 and §6 state insiders hold 77.1% and the free float is 27.4% [S0] — together 104.5% of the company, which cannot be right. S3 also shows the controller vehicle DIA at 8.33% immediately before the July 2025 rights issue, so the group stake needs reconciliation. The reader cannot determine the true free float, which matters for the 2% buyback and the liquidity assumption.
challenges.answer: The pack's insider 77.1% and free float 27.4% are dropped. Section 6 reconciles to the annual report: Sapta 45.29%, Dwimuria 19.95%, public 33.26%, treasury 1.5%; the report states the pack fields sum above the company and are not used [S3].

challenges.challenge: The summary compares 9M26 lease income of IDR8,679.5bn with 'IDR8,725.6bn for the whole of FY2025' (F11 vs F4) — a nine-month figure against a full-year segment line. The annual-report tower-rental line against the 9M25 comparative (8,503.1) implies a Rp222bn Q4 2025, impossible against a ~Rp2.9tn quarterly run-rate: the lines are not the same scope. The like-for-like move is +2.1% (F11), which the key-input basis states correctly.
challenges.answer: Scope corrected: consolidated lease income was 11,671.3 in FY2025 against 8,679.5 in 9M26 and 8,503.1 in 9M25, not the 8,725.6 tower-segment rental line. The comparison is now like-for-like nine months and the segment-scope difference is explained in sections 1 and 3 [S3][S4].

challenges.challenge: The towers card requires contract length, escalator terms (fixed vs inflation-linked) and renewal cliffs. The report asserts 'multi-year umbrella agreements' and an 'inflation-linked escalator' but never states a length, an escalator rate or the nearest renewal date, and the model has no tenancy driver — revenue is grown on a consolidated percentage. §5's signpost ('a tenancy ratio below our bear assumption') refers to an assumption that does not exist in the model.
challenges.answer: Section 2 now states the contract terms: XLSMART take-or-pay ten years, Berca master lease ten years per site with two extensions, no disclosed escalator, renewal cliffs beyond the explicit horizon. It also says plainly that the model has no tenancy driver because the quarterly LK does not disclose tower counts [S3][S4].

challenges.challenge: Terminal growth of 4.0% is 0.7% real over the deck's 3.28% CPI and far below the ~8.6% nominal GDP path (real 5.29 plus CPI 3.28) and the 5% house cap. The basis ('inflation plus a fraction of real data-traffic growth') does not source the 0.7pp. It is the second-largest lever: the §4 grid gives Rp823 at 5.0% vs Rp697 at 4.0%, +Rp126 a share and +Rp146 on the twelve-month target. A tower book with inflation-linked escalators growing at 0.7% real for ever is a judgement, not a sourced base case.
challenges.answer: Terminal growth cut to 3.5%: macro deck CPI 3.28% plus 0.2pp real, inside the 5% cap, with the basis stating that rent grew 2.1% in 9M26 and no escalator is disclosed, so even 3.5% assumes the tenancy slide stops [S4][S3].

challenges.challenge: The drift.capex_pct justification says FY2026E 34.0% 'is the actual nine-month ratio annualised' and then computes 4,146.4/11,060.1 = 37.5% in the same sentence. 34.0% is 3.5pp below the actual run-rate, so the base understates FY2026 capex by ~Rp520bn. The justification also says capex must 'converge on D&A (20.6%)', but the model leaves capex at 26.0% against D&A of 20.5% in FY2035E — the stated convergence never happens.
challenges.answer: FY2026 capex is set to the actual 37.5% of revenue (4,146.4 on 11,060.1), gliding to 26.0% by FY2030, and the basis now says outright that capex stays above D&A and does not converge; the false convergence claim is removed from section 3 [S4][S3].

challenges.challenge: The report never mentions the two same-name KILLs (T-INDO-TOWR-001/-002, 2026-08-24 and 2026-10-19) at 366-448 on a 6.66x P/E anchor, yet initiates BUY at Rp825 — 2.3x that fair value and 2.2x the last close — while FY2025 EPS fell to 63 from 67 and 9M26 lease income grew 2.1%. The reversal rests entirely on switching method to a DCF. Relatedly, the summary calls 825 the 'fundamental value', but the base-case DCF is Rp697; 825 is the probability-weighted blend that borrows Rp331/share from the 25% bull.
challenges.answer: The investment summary now names the two prior kills and what changed (method plus balance sheet), and it separates the 551 base-case DCF from the 728 probability-weighted target instead of calling the blend fundamental value [S0][S3].

challenges.challenge: §2 says 'industry consolidation among the tower operators has been discussed publicly … nothing has been announced [S3]', and the bull narrative's first driver is 'the mooted tower merger'. S3 does not discuss a tower-operator merger — its only TBIG reference is a Rp6,824 trade payable. The only pack source for the mooted MTEL-TBIG merger is S8, a beritasatu piece quoting an analyst's research note. S8 is not cited anywhere in the report (good), but its content has leaked into the bull driver and is misattributed to S3.
challenges.answer: The MTEL-TBIG tower merger was sourced only to S8, a press piece carrying broker commentary, which is barred. It is removed from the bull narrative and section 2, which now says no company, regulator or exchange announcement exists, so none is modelled [S3].

challenges.challenge: The dropped EV/EBITDA cross-check is the largest upside argument in the pack and is never stated. TOWR trades at 6.0x FY2026E EV/EBITDA, 5.9x P/E and 0.73x book against peer medians of 14.5x EV/EBITDA, 23.7x P/E (MTEL 12.6x, TBIG 15.6x) and 1.73x book. At TBIG's 11.7x — the least aggressive independent peer — fair value is ~Rp1,410; at 14.5x, ~Rp1,940. The report dismisses the set in one sentence and inverts the number instead of explaining the 2.4x gap.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now states the peer-gap upside explicitly: at roughly twice our forward EV/EBITDA the equity is worth about the 1,102 bull case, and at the peer median more, with the reason that gap is not in the base (four times levered, thinning float, falling margin) [S0].

challenges.challenge: 'The buyback … is IDR0.0bn' (F20 is Rp500bn; the idrb filter divides by 1,000). Rp500bn is ~2.3% of the current market cap, not zero, and the sentence's claim that it is 'small enough to support the price rather than retire a meaningful slice' is an opinion built on a misprinted number.
challenges.answer: The buyback placeholder now formats as 0.50tn instead of 0.0bn (idrb divided a figure already in IDR bn by a billion); both mentions in sections 3 and 6 are fixed [S5].

challenges.challenge: The DCF discounts the full FY2026E FCFF of 3,798 at t~0.005 (PV 3,796) while the bridge uses 30-Sep-2026 net debt of 45,527 and the model's own FY2026E net debt line is 43,368. Part of FY2026 has already been earned into that balance sheet, so the stub and the bridge are on different dates. The gross double count is ~Rp49/share, largely offset by using the 30-Sep rather than year-end net debt (~Rp37), but the convention is not stated and the value is not reproducible from the report.
challenges.answer: The DCF is stub-aware: the FY2026 row discounts 0.2519 of the year from the 30 September balance-sheet date, giving a FY2026E FCFF of 3,275.5 and 824.6 of present value rather than the full year, and the net-debt bridge uses 30 September net debt, so both sides sit on one date basis. Section 4 states that convention [S0].

missing_bull_case.note: Understated. FY2025 tenancy rose from 1.639x to 1.670x (58,035/35,400 to 60,540/36,247, the report's own F1/F2) and 9M26 revenue grew 14.2% (11,060.1 vs 9,686.7). The controller took its rights and stood standby at Rp680 in July 2025, 1.8x today's Rp370 (S3). The peer multiple gap (C14) is the largest single upside argument and is inverted, not stated.

missing_bear_case.note: Absent. The refinancing reset is not quantified: S4 shows 2026 rupiah loan rates to 8.69% against the 6.2% modelled; USD/JPY/CNH tranches are unhedged in the model under a balance_of_payments_pressure deck (USD/IDR 18,350 vs 18,063); the CIMB Rp2tn runs only to Oct-2027 (S6); and no services-reversal (project revenue) bear exists.

assumption_realism.note: Three value-moving drivers are not consistent with the facts: cost of debt 9.45% vs 6.2% effective and 4.65-8.69% disclosed (S4); terminal growth 4.0% vs the 5% cap; FY2026E capex 34.0% vs the 37.5% nine-month actual. FY2027 revenue of 15,748 also needs services +17.2%. Rent, margin and D&A otherwise tie to the 9M26 actuals.

evidence_and_citations.note: Facts F1-F23 and the S3/S4 quotes I spot-checked (tenancy, revenue split, EBITDA, D&A, cash flow, rights issue Rp680, customer percentages 38/32/11 = 81%) are accurate. But: peer median mislabelled 6.0x (own multiple, peers 14.5x); ownership 77.1%+27.4%=104.5%; 9M-vs-FY lease comparison; tower-merger claim cited to S3 when only S8 says it.

valuation_method_fit.note: A 100% FCFF DCF is defensible for a contracted annuity, but the towers card's own method is EV/EBITDA(AL) vs peers and own history cross-checked with AFFO yield vs the 10y FR. Both cross-checks are dropped, no AFFO yield is computed, and at the Rp825 target the FY2027 AFFO yield is ~7.4% against a 7.45% FR — no spread for 4x leverage. Stub/bridge date convention is also unreconciled (C16).

bias_and_tone.note: The prose says more than the evidence. 'Fundamental value Rp825' is the probability-weighted blend of a Rp697 base-case DCF; the 2.3x jump over the two same-name KILLs (366-448) is never discussed; the reverse DCF attributes the whole gap to tenancy decline while holding the analyst's own WACC and margin. Credit: doubling the bear weight (40/50/10) still gives ~Rp644, so the BUY conclusion itself survives.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: CPI 3.28% is used consistently in terminal growth and the 10y FR is the deck's rf, but the macro deck is read only through the rate path: the CAUTIOUS balance_of_payments_pressure regime and USD/IDR 18,350 are not carried into the USD/JPY/CNH debt or any FX sensitivity, and the 9.45% cost of debt is a deck default (rf + 2.0pp), not TOWR's disclosed rate.

conservatism_audit.note: Unjustified caution: kd 9.45% (worth roughly Rp400+ a share), terminal g 4.0% vs 5% cap (+Rp126), capex glide to 26% against D&A 20.5%, FY2026E revenue held at a flat Q4. Unjustified optimism: services +17.2% implied, FY2026E capex below the actual run-rate. Shocks are properly mirrored (two each, +/-3pp growth, +/-1.5pp margin); the bear is wrongly applied to FY2026E.

calibration.note: The margin gate is properly justified and I verified the arithmetic: FY2025A 79.3% (7,497.7+3,073.3 on 13,327.9), 9M26 73.4% (5,690.9+2,428.7 on 11,060.1). Credit. But the drift.capex_pct BLOCK justification calls 34.0% 'the nine-month ratio annualised' while computing 4,146.4/11,060.1=37.5% in the same sentence — a BLOCK justification must match the model it defends.

signoff.notes: All 16 MATERIAL challenges answered on substance (13 accepted with report fixes, 3 rebutted with sourced reasoning); QC round 2 PASS with neutral bias. Base case anchors on 9M26 actuals (73.3% margin held, 37.5% capex, Q3 run-rate Q4), scenarios mirrored, AFFO clears the 7.4% FR. TOWR is the only BUY in the tower batch with a sourced reason: 6.0x EV/EBITDA vs 8.8-18.9x peers after a Rp5.5tn rights issue cut net debt to 3.7x and a 10-year XLSMART take-or-pay locks rent. Two NOTEs (F41 rounding, dps basis) are cosmetic and non-blocking.

bias.note: Base case is anchored on the last actuals, not caution: FY2026E holds the 9M26 margin of 73.3% with no recovery, FY2026E revenue is the nine-month actual plus Q4 at the Q3 run-rate (11,060.1 + 3,854.5 = 14,914.6 against 13,327.9), FY2026E capex is the actual 37.5% ratio, and terminal growth 3.5% = CPI 3.28 plus 0.2pp real, inside the cap. The two conservative departures are disclosed and sourced: pre-tax cost of debt 9.45% sits above the LK rupiah ceiling of 8.69% [S4], argued in section 4 as a forward marginal rate while the LK book rate is 6.2%, and FY2027 growth of 4.0% against 9M26 14.2% assumes services project revenue flat and rent up 2%, consistent with 9M26 rent growth of 2.1% [S4 note 37]. Both are offset by a 30% bull weight larger than the 20% bear. No unsupported haircut found; scenarios are mirrored on the same three shocks (growth 3pp, gross margin 1.5pp, WACC 0.5pp) and probabilities sum to 100% with base at 50%.

findings.finding: Section 5 still renders the dollar-book rate sensitivity as IDR0.00tn (the round-1 Q6 note, unfixed). F41 is 2.852bn so the figure is right but the formatting rounds it away and reads as zero risk, the opposite of the intended point.

The model dps history line is on a cash-paid calendar basis (FY2022A 24.1, FY2025A 6.89) while section 3 quotes declared-for-the-year figures (FY2023 24.1, FY2024 15.9, FY2025 TTM 13.76) and the 22% payout rests on those. The prose is self-consistent and sourced [S3 p.16][S0], but a reader comparing the dps row with section 3 sees an apparent 10.9% payout in FY2025A against the 22% assumed.

flags.message: FY+1 ebitda margin moves -6.0pp from FY2025A: source the change
flags.justification: The fall is in the reported nine-month figures, not a forecast haircut. On the restated basis FY2025A EBITDA margin is 79.3% (operating profit 7,497.7 plus D&A 3,073.3 on revenue 13,327.9) [S3 p.462, note 32], while nine months 2026 gives 73.4% (operating profit 5,690.9 plus D&A 2,428.7 on 11,060.1) [S4 p.7, note 38]. The gap is mix: services and other revenue doubled to 2,245.9 while lease income grew only 2.1%, so other cost of revenues rose 98% to 1,593.5 on a base whose D&A did not move [S4 note 37]. FY2026E 73.3% holds the nine-month actual and nothing further is deducted.

flags.message: a.capex_pct moves -11.5pp from FY2026E to FY2035E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: FY2026E 37.5% is the actual nine-month ratio: payments for fixed assets and supplier advances 4,146.4 on revenue 11,060.1 = 37.5% [S4 cash-flow statement]. The glide to 26.0% by FY2035E is the completion of the 2026 tower, fibre and power build, not a cut below maintenance: FY2025 realised capex was 23.9% of revenue [S3 p.181], so the terminal ratio stays above the last pre-cycle actual and above D&A of 20.5%, because the group keeps building for growth. The previous version cut FY2026E to 34.0% while its own arithmetic gave 37.5%; this fixes that and states plainly that capex does not converge on D&A.

flags.message: expected return +101%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The gap to the last close comes from three sourced drivers, not a re-rating. First the contracted cash flow: lease income is 11,671.3 in FY2025 and 8,679.5 in nine months of 2026, and the XLSMART take-or-pay runs ten years [S3 note 31, p.621][S4 note 37]. Second the balance sheet: the July 2025 rights issue raised 5,496.8 and was pushed down to Protelindo to repay debt, taking net debt to last-quarter-annualised EBITDA from 4.6x to 3.7x [S3 p.14, p.10], and the rupiah floating-rate sensitivity is 242.9 per 100bp, so a full reset to the 8.69% ceiling is material but not existential [S4 note 43]. Third the price: at 370 the shares are about 0.7x book and 5.6x forward earnings, and the reverse DCF shows the market requiring FY2027 revenue growth of 2.1% against our 4.0% [S0]. The value is a ten-year DCF at the house 10.28% WACC and 3.5% terminal growth; the sensitivity grid in section 4 is where the honest risk sits.

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.6, 'ev_ebitda': 0.3, 'div_yield': 0.1}
flags.justification: Both cross-checks are dropped and shown as arithmetic rather than blended. The peer EV/EBITDA median is 14.5x on three names (BALI, CENT, TBIG): CENT prints 37.6x from a small, heavily levered model, MTEL and IBST carry no EV/EBITDA in the pack, and excluding CENT the median is 13.1x [S0]. At TBIG's 11.7x on our FY2026E EBITDA of 10,941.7 the enterprise value is about 128.4tn; after 30-Sep-2026 net debt of 45.5tn, minorities of 0.7tn and associates of 0.4tn that is about Rp1,410 a share — roughly a quarter above the bull case of Rp1,102, not level with it — and at the 13.1x median excluding CENT about Rp1,660; we do not blend that re-rating into a base case when the company is four times levered with a thinning free float. The dividend yield cannot anchor value either: the payout is 22% of earnings [S3 p.16], so capitalising a 3.7% trailing yield at a peer median near 6% would value a distribution policy, not the business. The AFFO test is run in section 4 instead.
